concepts.name: The multiplication principle
concepts.description: If a task is done in stages, multiply the number of ways to do each stage to find the total.

concepts.name: The addition principle
concepts.description: If a choice is either one mutually exclusive option or another, add the number of ways for each.

concepts.name: Arranging distinct items
concepts.description: n distinct items can be arranged in a row in n! (n factorial) ways.

concepts.name: Repetition allowed or not
concepts.description: Whether a symbol can be reused changes the count at every later stage of the task.

concepts.name: Counting with restrictions
concepts.description: Treat items that must stay together as a single block, or count the complement when items must stay apart.

formulas.title: The multiplication principle
formulas.prompt: How do you count a task done in several independent stages?
formulas.formula: If stage 1 can be done in m ways and stage 2 in n ways, the whole task can be done in m × n ways
formulas.explanation: This extends to any number of stages: multiply the number of options at each one.
formulas.commonMistake: Adding the stage counts instead of multiplying them.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A restaurant has 4 starters and 3 mains. How many meals are possible?

formulas.title: The addition principle
formulas.prompt: How do you count when a choice is either one option or a completely separate one?
formulas.formula: If a choice can be made in m ways OR in n mutually exclusive ways, the total is m + n
formulas.explanation: Use addition only when the two sets of options do not overlap and only one is chosen.
formulas.example: 3 soups or 2 salads as a starter: 3 + 2 = 5 starter choices
formulas.commonMistake: Multiplying mutually exclusive choices instead of adding them.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A menu offers 3 soups or 2 salads as a starter. How many starter choices are there?

formulas.title: Arranging n distinct items
formulas.prompt: In how many ways can n distinct items be arranged in a row?
formulas.explanation: Each position removes one item from the choices for the next position.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting that the number of choices decreases by one at each position.
formulas.applicationPrompt: In how many ways can 4 distinct books be arranged on a shelf?

formulas.title: With or without repetition
formulas.prompt: How does allowing repetition change a counting problem?
formulas.formula:
With repetition, r positions from n symbols: nʳ
Without repetition: n × (n−1) × … × (n−r+1)
formulas.explanation: Without repetition, the number of remaining choices shrinks by one at every position; with repetition, it stays at n throughout.
formulas.example: 3-digit code from 10 digits: with repetition 10³ = 1,000; without repetition 10×9×8 = 720
formulas.commonMistake: Using the same formula for both cases.
formulas.applicationPrompt: How many 3-digit codes are possible from 10 digits if repetition is not allowed?

formulas.title: Items that must (or must not) stay together
formulas.prompt: How do you count arrangements where certain items must sit together?
formulas.formula: Treat the group that must stay together as one block; arrange the blocks, then arrange the items inside the block
formulas.explanation: For items that must NOT be together, it is often easier to count the total arrangements and subtract the ones where they are together.
formulas.example: 5 people, 2 must sit together: treat them as 1 block → 4 units to arrange (4!) × 2 ways to arrange the pair = 48
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting to multiply by the arrangements within the block.
formulas.applicationPrompt: In how many ways can 5 people be seated in a row if two specific people must sit together?

formulas.title: Count what you do not want
formulas.prompt: "At least one" counts are long. What is quicker?
formulas.explanation: "None" is usually a single product, while "at least one" splits into many cases.
formulas.commonMistake: Counting "exactly one 7" and calling it "at least one".
formulas.applicationPrompt: How many 4-digit numbers have at least one repeated digit?

formulas.title: When 0 is among the digits
formulas.prompt: Forming numbers from digits that include 0: what changes?
formulas.formula:
Fill the first place first: it has one choice fewer (no 0).
Then fill the rest.
formulas.explanation: A number cannot start with 0, so the leading place is the restricted one.
formulas.commonMistake: Writing 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 = 360, which includes numbers starting with 0.
formulas.applicationPrompt: How many 3-digit even numbers can be made from 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 without repeating?

levels.title: Counting Without Listing
levels.description: Multiplying and adding choices to count outcomes without writing every one out.

blocks.title: Stages multiply, alternatives add
blocks.body: Choosing a starter AND a main is a sequence of stages: multiply the choices (4 × 3 = 12). Choosing a starter OR a salad, never both, is a set of alternatives: add the choices (3 + 2 = 5).

blocks.title: The multiplication principle
blocks.body: Stage 1 (m ways) then Stage 2 (n ways) → m × n
blocks.caption: Use this whenever a task happens in a sequence of independent steps.

blocks.body: "And" usually means multiply; "or" (for mutually exclusive choices) usually means add.

levels.title: Fundamental Principle of Counting Formulas
levels.description: Multiplication and addition principles, factorial arrangements, repetition, restricted arrangements.

levels.title: Direct Counting
levels.description: Applying the multiplication and addition principles, and factorial arrangements.

levels.title: Combining Principles
levels.description: Mixing addition and multiplication, repetition, and simple restrictions.

levels.title: Mixed Fundamental Principle of Counting Practice

questions.question: A restaurant has 4 starters and 3 mains. How many ways can a diner choose one starter and one main?
questions.method: Multiply the number of choices at each stage.

hints.text: This is two independent stages, one after the other.

questions.question: A shirt comes in 3 colours and 4 sizes. How many colour-size combinations are there?

hints.text: Colour and size are chosen independently.

commonMistakes: Adding the two counts instead of multiplying.

questions.question: When two choices are "either-or" and never happen together, the total count is found by

options.text: subtracting the smaller from the larger

questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive either-or choices are combined by addition, not multiplication.
questions.method: Addition is for either-or; multiplication is for stage-by-stage tasks.

hints.text: Think of choosing a starter that is either a soup or a salad, never both.

questions.question: In how many ways can 4 distinct books be arranged on a shelf?
questions.method: Multiply n, then n−1, down to 1.

questions.question: A password uses 1 letter (from 26) followed by 1 digit (from 10). How many passwords are possible?
questions.method: Multiply the choices for each character position.

hints.text: Each position is an independent stage.

questions.question: A menu offers 3 soups or 2 salads as a starter (never both), followed by one of 4 mains. How many starter-main combinations are there?
questions.method: Add the mutually exclusive starter options, then multiply by the mains.

hints.text: Combine the starter options first with addition.

commonMistakes: Multiplying the soup and salad counts together.

questions.question: How many 3-digit codes can be formed from the digits 0–9 if repetition is allowed?
questions.explanation: Each of the 3 positions has 10 choices: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000.
questions.method: With repetition, every position has the same number of choices.

hints.text: Repetition means the count does not shrink at each position.

commonMistakes: Reducing the choices at each position as if repetition were not allowed.

questions.question: How many 3-digit codes can be formed from the digits 0–9 if repetition is not allowed?
questions.method: Each position removes one digit from the choices for the next.

hints.text: The number of choices shrinks by one at each position.

commonMistakes: Using 10 × 10 × 10 as if repetition were allowed.

questions.question: In how many ways can 5 people be seated in a row if two specific people must sit together?
questions.explanation: Treat the pair as one block: 4 units to arrange (4! = 24), and 2 ways to arrange the pair inside the block. Total: 24 × 2 = 48.
questions.method: Treat the pair as a single block, then arrange within it.

hints.text: Do not forget the pair can swap places inside their block.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to multiply by the 2 internal arrangements of the pair.

questions.question: A code has 2 letters (from 26, repetition allowed) followed by 2 digits (from 10, repetition allowed). How many codes are possible?
questions.method: Multiply the counts for every stage, in order.

hints.text: Combine the letter stages and digit stages separately, then multiply.

commonMistakes: Adding the letter and digit counts instead of multiplying.

questions.question: In how many ways can 6 people be arranged in a row if 3 specific people must NOT all sit together?
questions.explanation: Total arrangements: 6! = 720. Arrangements with all 3 together (as a block): treat as 1 block + 3 others = 4 units (4! = 24), times 3! = 6 ways inside the block, giving 144. Subtract: 720 − 144 = 576.
questions.method: Count the total, then subtract the arrangements where the restriction is violated.

hints.text: It is easier to count the complement (all together) and subtract.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to multiply by 3! for the internal arrangements of the block.

questions.question: How many 4-digit numbers greater than 5000 can be formed using the digits 1–9 without repetition?
questions.explanation: The first digit must be 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 (5 choices) to be greater than 5000. The remaining 3 digits come from the 8 leftover digits without repetition: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. Total: 5 × 336 = 1,680.
questions.method: Fix the restricted position first, then count the remaining positions without repetition.

hints.text: Decide the first digit's choices before counting the rest.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that the first digit is restricted, and using 9 choices for it.

questions.question: 5 people sit in a row. In how many arrangements are two specific people NOT adjacent?
questions.explanation: Total arrangements: 5! = 120. Arrangements with the two together (as a block): 4! × 2 = 48. Not adjacent: 120 − 48 = 72.
questions.method: Count the total, then subtract the arrangements where they are adjacent.
commonMistakes: Trying to directly count the non-adjacent arrangements instead of using the complement.
